title: Two piles
hookLine: before his awakening he sorted his thoughts into two kinds (MN 19)
carry: a path worn across a field

lines: AN EXPERIMENT ON HIS OWN MIND.
cards: Cleaning out a closet usually comes down to two piles: keep, and let go. You pick up a sweater, hold it for a second, and drop it on one side or the other. It's slow at first.
After an hour you're fast, because your hands have learned what belongs where.
In one sutta the Buddha looks back to the years before his awakening, when he was still searching, and tells the monks about a simple experiment he ran on his own mind. Two piles.

teach.b: The sutta is number nineteen in the Middle-Length Discourses, and its name means two kinds of thought.
Before my awakening, the Buddha says, while I was still a bodhisatta, it occurred to me: what if I divide my thoughts into two classes?
On one side, thoughts of sensual desire, of ill will, and of cruelty. On the other: thoughts of letting go, of goodwill, and of harmlessness. That second pile is exactly yesterday's right intention.
When a thought from the first pile came up, he saw where it led: to his own affliction, to others' affliction, to both. It blocked wisdom and led away from peace.
And as he considered that, the sutta says, the thought subsided, and he let it go. A thought from the second pile led to no one's harm, and helped wisdom grow. Then comes a line worth carrying home.
Whatever someone keeps thinking about and pondering, the Buddha says, that becomes the leaning of their mind.

teach.h: WHAT YOU PONDER, THE MIND LEANS TO.
teach.b: Think often about ill will, and the mind leans toward ill will. Think often about goodwill, and it leans toward goodwill. Like a path worn across a field, or a closet that sorts itself faster every time.
The method is humble. No special state required. Just noticing which pile a thought belongs in, and where it's heading.
A practice from before the awakening, offered to anyone.

how: Some Buddhist meditation teachers teach students to notice thoughts as wholesome or unwholesome and to see where they lead, a method drawn from the Dvedhavitakka Sutta.

o: splitting good people from bad people
dividing your day into work and rest
sorting thoughts by whether they lead to harm

p: the sutta of two kinds of thought

s: the two-piles practice comes from after the Buddha's awakening
he says he did it before, while still a bodhisatta.
the second pile matches the three parts of right intention
in MN 19, an unwholesome thought subsided once he saw where it led
he considered that it led to affliction and away from wisdom, and it subsided; then he let it go.

games.q: you're the bodhisatta, sorting your thoughts. a thought of ill will comes up. what do you do, in the sutta?
o: see that it leads to harm for you and others, and let it fade.
follow it through to see what happens.
games.why: he saw that it led to his own and others' affliction and away from wisdom, and as he saw that, it subsided.

practice: Watch thoughts come and go, and as each one passes, set it gently on a side: wanting, resentment or harm in the first pile; letting go, goodwill or kindness in the second. If you can't tell, let it pass unsorted.
Don't argue with any thought; just notice which way it leans.

wordCard.voice: Two piles. The Buddha's practice before awakening: sorting thoughts into those that lead to harm and those that lead to good, because the mind leans toward what it ponders.

orig.note: Pali dvedhāvitakka: two kinds of thought, the title of MN 19; vitakka means thought.

carryVoice: Your line: a path worn across a field. What the mind keeps returning to, it leans toward. That's day three hundred sixty.

sources.ref: MN 19 (Dvedhavitakka Sutta, two kinds of thought)
